metadata.title: Password Authentication with Insecure Communication
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: PDF first page matches metadata title 'Password Authentication with Insecure Communication' by Lamport (1981).

nodes.name: Password Authentication over an Insecure Channel
nodes.statement: Authenticate a remote user via password while protecting against (1) intruders reading the system's stored data, and (2) intruders intercepting communications between user and system.
nodes.statement_clean: Design a password authentication scheme that is secure even if the system's data is exposed and the channel is wiretapped or tampered with.

nodes.name: One-Way Function
nodes.statement: A mapping $F$ from a set of words into itself such that (1) given $x$, it is easy to compute $F(x)$, and (2) given $y$, it is not feasible to compute $x$ such that $y = F(x)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A function easy to evaluate forward but infeasible to invert.

nodes.name: Constructing $F$ from a Secure Encryption Algorithm
nodes.statement: A one-way function $F$ can be built from a secure encryption algorithm by computing $F(x)$ as the encryption of a standard word using $x$ as the key.
nodes.statement_clean: Use symmetric encryption of a fixed plaintext under key $x$ to realize $F(x)$.

nodes.name: Stored-Hash Password Authentication
nodes.statement: Standard scheme: store $y = F(x)$ instead of $x$; on login compute $F(x)$ from submitted $x$ and compare to $y$.
output: Accept/reject decision based on comparing $F(x)$ to stored $y$

nodes.name: Eavesdropping Weakness of Stored-Hash Scheme
nodes.statement: Storing $y = F(x)$ defeats data-disclosure attacks but does NOT prevent eavesdropping: an adversary on the line can capture $x$ and replay it.
nodes.statement_clean: Hashing the stored value alone is not enough against wiretappers.

nodes.name: Password Sequence $x_1, \ldots, x_{1000}$
nodes.statement: A sequence of one-time passwords where $x_i$ is used for the $i$th login. The system stores $y_i = F(x_i)$ for verification, and the $y_i$ must be distinct to prevent replay.

nodes.name: Generation/Storage of the Password Sequence
nodes.statement: Devise a scheme to choose and maintain $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{1000}$ avoiding the drawbacks of (a) storing all 1000 values on user and system, and (b) sending each next $y_{i+1}$ during the $i$th session (which is not robust to communication failure).

nodes.name: Iterated One-Way Function $F^n$
nodes.statement: $F^n$ denotes $n$ successive applications of $F$, i.e., $F^n(x) = F(F(\cdots F(x)\cdots))$ ($n$ times).

nodes.name: Hash-Chain Password Construction
nodes.statement: For a fixed secret word $x$, define the $i$th password as $x_i = F^{1000-i}(x)$, so the password sequence is $F^{999}(x), \ldots, F(F(x)), F(x), x$.
nodes.statement_clean: Passwords are released in reverse iteration order along a chain $F^{999}(x), \ldots, F(x), x$.

nodes.name: Authentication Recurrence $y_i = x_{i-1}$
nodes.statement: From $x_i = F^{1000-i}(x)$ it follows that $y_i = F(x_i) = x_{i-1}$ for $i > 1$; equivalently, each user password equals the value the system needs to authenticate the next one.

nodes.name: Lamport Hash-Chain Authentication
nodes.statement: Authentication scheme where the system stores only the last accepted password and accepts $x_i$ iff $F(x_i)$ equals the stored value.
output: Accept iff $F(x_i)$ equals the stored value (which is $x_{i-1}$ for $i>1$, or $y_1$ for $i=1$)
After acceptance, system updates its stored value to $x_i$

nodes.name: Distinctness of $y_i$
nodes.statement: The values $y_i = F^{1000-i+1}(x)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, 1000$ are distinct, since otherwise $F^{987}(x) = F^{123}(x)$ (say) would let an adversary invert $F$ on $y' = F^{123}(x)$.
assumptions: $x$ chosen so that the chain has length $\le 1000$
conclusions: All $y_i$ in the password sequence are pairwise distinct

nodes.name: Security against Eavesdropping/Tampering
nodes.statement: Knowing the first $k$ passwords $F^{999}(x), \ldots, F^{1000-k}(x)$ does not enable an intruder to compute $F^{999-k}(x)$; otherwise one could invert $F$ on $y' = F^{1000-k}(x)$, contradicting one-wayness.
assumptions: Adversary may eavesdrop or tamper with the channel
conclusions: No amount of channel observation lets the adversary impersonate the user or permanently lock him out

nodes.name: Proof of Eavesdropping Security
nodes.statement: By contradiction: assume knowing $F^{999}(x), \ldots, F^{13}(x)$ enables computing $F^{12}(x)$; then given $y' = F^{13}(x)$ one can compute $F^{14}(x), \ldots, F^{19}(x)$ and ultimately $x' = F^{12}(x)$ with $y' = F(x')$, contradicting property 2 of $F$.

nodes.name: Robustness via Resynchronization
nodes.statement: If user and system are out of sync (user sends $x_j$ while system holds $y_k$ with $j \ne k$), repeatedly applying $F$ to the password and to the system's value until they match detects the offset; e.g. $x_j = F^2(y_{j+3})$ when the system is three steps ahead.

nodes.name: Crash Recovery by Jumping Forward
nodes.statement: After a system crash the system can be 'jumped forward' instead of backed up: e.g. if recovery point holds $y_{374} = F^{626}(x)$ and at most one identification per hour is allowed, requesting $x_{376}$ is safe because $y_{374} = F^3(x_{376})$, so a recorded $x_{374}$ cannot be reused.

nodes.name: Microcomputer-in-Terminal Implementation
nodes.statement: User picks $x$ at random and uses a local mode of an intelligent terminal to compute $F(x), F^2(x), \ldots, F^{1000}(x)$; the final value $F^{1000}(x)$ is delivered tamper-proof (e.g. carried physically) to the system, and during login the terminal computes $x_i = F^{1000-i}(x)$ from $x$ and the system-supplied index $i$.

nodes.name: Time-Memory Tradeoff for Chain Computation
nodes.statement: Recomputation of $x_i$ can be avoided by storing intermediate values $x, F^k(x), F^{2k}(x), \ldots$ for some $k$, e.g. on a removable storage device, trading storage for online computation.

nodes.name: Periodic Re-keying after 1000 Uses
nodes.statement: After 1000 authentications the user must choose a new $x$ and rerun the setup; relying on a single secret indefinitely is in any case unsound.
